source.title: Pre-training under infinite compute
source.authors: Konwoo Kim; Suhas Kotha; Percy Liang; Tatsunori Hashimoto

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study’s own scaling experiments report overfitting in standard recipes and monotone loss decrease after regularization, refining or challenging the predicted double-descent pattern.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are scaling sweeps reported in text and figures; the plotted loss values are not transcribed numerically in the text. The paper also discusses prior double-descent results, but those cited findings are not rows. Its data-scaling experiments do not specifically test increasing sample size near an interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps model size and epoch count for Llama-style LMs on a fixed 200M-token pool. It reports a non-monotone validation loss under default weight decay and monotone loss once regularization is jointly tuned, and it frames this explicitly against double descent. This is a new setting (data-constrained LM pre-training) with its own results on V1, V2 and V6. It is better described as T3 than T5: the authors present the result as agreeing with optimal-regularization theory, not as refuting a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that standard data-constrained recipes overfit with too many epochs or parameters. Jointly tuning weight decay (up to 30× the default), LR and epochs gives monotone power-law scaling in parameter count. They state this agrees with theory that optimally tuned regularization makes loss monotone even where double descent would occur. They attribute the rise to overfitting tentatively and never claim to observe a double-descent curve.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Llama-style autoregressive language-model pre-training on fixed web-text pools, measuring held-out validation loss while sweeping model size and epochs and tuning regularization; it does not reproduce the original double-descent setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The model-size trend changes with regularization: the standard recipe eventually overfits, whereas jointly tuning weight decay, learning rate, and epoch count yields monotone loss decrease. Epoch count also affects the onset of overfitting.
record.problems: The claim-relevant scaling evidence is for a limited set of model sizes and a 200M-token training pool. The authors do not locate an interpolation threshold, and they describe the attribution of rising loss to overfitting as likely or hypothesized. They also note that the 1.4B model has non-standard depth/width scaling. The relevant plotted losses are not given numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the broader seed-token scaling results: those experiments do not specifically test whether more samples raise error near an interpolation threshold. Cited results from prior work were also excluded.

untested.parts: Location of a peak relative to the size that just fits the training set; any second descent beyond 1.4B.
A second descent over training time; within-run test-loss trajectories (only end-of-training losses are reported).
Role of label noise; triple or multiple descent; evidence that the observed rise is a double-descent peak rather than ordinary overfitting.
No sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.

missing.what: Ablation: weight decay fixed at the 150M optimum (0.8) across sizes gives non-monotone size scaling, while per-size tuning gives monotone scaling. This shows the peak's disappearance needs optimally tuned, not merely larger, regularization.
Standard recipe across 200M, 400M, 800M and 1.6B tokens: 600M slightly beats 1.4B at every token count, so the size-wise rise recurs across data scales.
Heavy weight decay shifts the epoch-wise overfitting point right and down, for both validation loss and downstream benchmarks.
Train loss falls monotonically with epochs while validation loss rises; at fixed 4 epochs, train loss falls with size while validation loss rises.
Downstream accuracy under the unregularized size sweep is non-monotone (600M avg 53.42% vs 300M 55.34%), while the regularized sweep rises monotonically to 60.73% at 1.4B.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. The double-descent link rests on a narrow sweep: four sizes on one token budget. The 'peak' is not shown to sit at an interpolation threshold; train loss is not near zero by the authors' account, and the rise may be ordinary overfitting. The V6 support should therefore be read as 'non-monotone scaling vanishes under tuned regularization', not as confirming a double-descent peak. All losses are figure-only except asymptotes (3.43 regularized) and a few distillation numbers.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not locate a model size that just fits the training set or establish that any peak is near that point.
It reports epoch-related overfitting, but does not establish a full fall-rise-fall curve over training time.
No targeted sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold to test whether more training samples raise test error.
No comparison across general model classes; the experiments use Llama-style autoregressive language models.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
The study tests regularization effects on scaling and overfitting, but does not test whether label noise drives a peak or whether triple or multiple descent occurs.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to determine whether a second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: 300M parameter Llama-style model
rows.operation_detail: Varied epoch count for the fixed-data standard recipe.
rows.measure: Held-out validation loss across epoch counts
rows.note: The text says repeating data initially lowers loss, but sufficiently high epoch counts lead to overfitting and rising loss. It does not report a subsequent fall.
rows.check: Each epoch count is a separate run whose cosine schedule anneals to zero, so the x-axis is total repetitions, not a within-run training-time trajectory. Only fall-then-rise is shown (up to 128 epochs); no second fall. Value is figure-only.

source_check.correct: For V2, state=cannot_determine. Epoch counts compare separate runs evaluated after their own learning-rate schedules anneal to zero. The endpoint sweep shows initial improvement followed by overfitting, but does not establish a within-run fall-rise-fall trajectory.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.1; Figure 2 left; Appendix A, learning-rate schedule.
source_check.problem: A partial endpoint pattern is recorded as partial evidence for a claim about loss over training time.

rows.subject: Standard pre-training model-size sweep (150M, 300M, 600M, 1.4B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count and tuned epoch count and learning rate for each size.
rows.measure: Held-out validation loss across model sizes
rows.note: The authors report that loss starts increasing as parameter count grows despite tuning, and that the 1.4B model performs worse than the 600M model. They do not report a second descent.
rows.check: Four sizes only (150M–1.4B). Loss barely improves, and 1.4B is worse than 600M, so only a rise is seen. No interpolation threshold is located, so whether a second descent would follow at larger N cannot be judged. The 1.4B model also has non-standard depth/width, a confound the authors flag.

rows.subject: Regularized pre-training model-size sweep (150M, 300M, 600M, 1.4B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count after jointly tuning weight decay, learning rate, and epoch count at each size.
rows.measure: Held-out validation loss across model sizes
rows.uncertainty: The authors report asymptote variation of at most 0.02 loss across 3 seeds.
rows.note: The authors describe the regularized loss as monotonically decreasing with parameter count, without a reported peak or second descent.
rows.check: For V6 the state is observed: the non-monotonicity disappears under jointly tuned weight decay. For V1 the state is absent (no peak). A single state field cannot hold both, and the V6 reading is recorded here. The uncertainty field (asymptote variation ≤0.02 across 3 seeds) refers to the power-law asymptote, not to the per-point losses.

source_check.correct: For V1, state=absent: the tuned size sweep decreases monotonically without a peak or second descent. For the regularization-dependence component of V6, state=observed: joint tuning removes the standard recipe's nonmonotonicity. Neither a double-descent peak nor its interpolation threshold is established.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3; Figure 3 and its hyperparameter table; Appendix B.2.
source_check.problem: The shared observed state does not fit both linked versions.

relationships.condition: Standard recipe (wd 0.1, tuned LR and epochs), 200M tokens, 150M–1.4B
relationships.reason: Loss rises past 600M with no recovery up to 1.4B (r2). Because no threshold is located, this shows only the rising part of the curve, in a narrow size range.
relationships.display_finding: Loss increased beyond 600M parameters without recovery through 1.4B, while the interpolation threshold remained undetermined.

statements.problem: The conditions and endpoint pattern are accurate, but the limits_scope classification treats separate annealed endpoints as a test of within-run epoch-wise double descent.

statements.correction: Regularization-relevant size sweep: 150M, 300M, 600M and 1.4B parameters. Noise causation and multiple peaks untested. No established interpolation threshold or double-descent peak. No instruct/chat-stage test.
statements.problem: The metadata-based size gap is misleading for this study: its regularization comparison explicitly resolves a 1.4B model. The caveats about noise causation, multiplicity and unidentified double descent remain valid.
